public_rationale: Both parts hold. A Science study found AI-assisted coding in the US rose from about 5% of new code in 2022 to nearly 30% by late 2024, so LLMs were coding more. On security, Veracode's July 2025 tests found vulnerabilities in 45% of cases and said models were improving at accuracy but not at security. A December 2025 agent benchmark found that only 10.5% of solutions were secure, even though 61% worked. As of the post, the evidence did not show that AI-generated code was secure or trustworthy. Instead it documented frequent flaws, so saying 'it's not clear' is accurate.
limitations: The code-share figure covers open-source Python on GitHub only.
The security evidence comes from test tasks: a vendor report and a preprint later accepted at ICML 2026.

our_interpretation: Two parts: (a) LLMs are writing a growing share of code; (b) the security and trustworthiness of that code had not been established as of the post.

Ongoing-state claim with no named period. The target period runs from late 2024 to the post date: the most recent data on AI's share of code available before the post covered late 2024 and early 2025, and the security studies date from 2025.
Part (b) is a claim of uncertainty. Studies showing frequent vulnerabilities support it. Strong evidence that AI code is reliably secure would contradict it.
criteria.support_condition: Data show the share of code written with AI rising, and credible studies show AI-generated code frequently has security flaws, so its trustworthiness is not established.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Data show AI coding is not growing, or credible evidence before the post shows AI-generated code is reliably secure and trustworthy.
